title: host-device-path-impact-kv-warmups
summary: Working notes and experiment log for measuring how host-device interconnect topology (PCIe Gen4/Gen5 vs NVLink meshes) affects KV-cache warmup behavior, tail latency spikes, and throughput stability for long-context streaming inference on A100/H100/L40S cloud SKUs.
hypothesis: If host-device path bandwidth/latency is the primary contributor to early-request latency variance during KV warmup, then SKUs with NVLink (or similar high-bandwidth device-local fabrics) will show faster convergence to steady-state per-request latency and fewer p99 spikes compared with PCIe-only SKUs. Conversely, PCIe Gen5 SKUs may match NVLink for throughput at steady-state but show worse transient behavior during cache population and eviction events.
test_plan: 1) Run identical streaming inference workload (token-at-a-time, incremental KV population) across representative SKUs: A100 (PCIe4), H100 (NVLink or PCIe variants), L40S (PCIe5 where available). 2) Synthetic and real prompts: a) repeated short prompts to warm model but not KV, b) long conversation sequences to exercise KV population, c) mixed-size traffic to emulate PLG bursts. 3) Instrument: measure host<->device memcpy latencies, kernel launch latency distribution, CUDA stream congestion, and per-request end-to-end latency (client-end). 4) Collect hardware counters (PCIe throughput, NVLink counters when available), nvidia-smi telemetry, and CUPTI traces for representative segments. 5) Repeat across driver/CUDA combos: CUDA 12.1 + drivers X, CUDA 12.2 + drivers Y (explicit labels in results).
hardware_matrix:
SKUs tested: 
- cloud-a: A100 PCIe (aws p4d-style) - CUDA 12.2 / driver 545.x 
- cloud-b: H100 NVLink (aws p5d-style) - CUDA 12.2 / driver 545.x 
- cloud-c: H100 PCIe variant (no NVLink) - CUDA 12.1 / driver 535.x 
- cloud-d: L40S PCIe Gen5 (gcp-like) - CUDA 12.2 / driver 545.x 
Notes: machines matched for CPU (16 vCPU) and RAM (~512GB) to minimize host-side bottleneck variability. Kernel driver versions were chosen to reflect common provider images in the wild.
workloads_and_models:
- Model: 13B transformer baseline (same quantization and torchscript runtimes across systems) to keep kernel selection consistent.
- Modes: FP16 and GPTQ-8-bit simulated quantization (we used Redwood's quantized runtime to ensure same compute graph).
- Request patterns: single-client streaming at 1 req/sec ramp to 50 req/sec; batch sizes 1 to 8; context lengths from 128 to 8192 tokens.
- KV pattern: streaming conversation where each new user message appends 512 tokens on average, forcing repeated KV extension and occasional eviction (when context exceeds soft cap).
instrumentation:
- CUPTI traces for selected streaming windows (capture kernel launch timestamps and mem copies).
- Custom host-side probe that timestamps host memcpy start/end and first kernel invocation after memcpy.
- nvidia-smi logging (every 200ms) for GPU utilization, memory used, and PCIe/NVLink traffic where exposed.
- perf + ftrace on host to ensure there is no CPU-side stall causing memcpy lag.
- Application-level markers (start_request, kv_append, first_token_out) to compute warmup interval = first_token_out - start_request for cold-to-warm transitions.
results_summary:
High-level observations from the runs: 
- NVLink H100 (cloud-b) consistently reached steady-state median latency ~8-12% faster during first 20 tokens of long-context streams compared to PCIe-only A100 (cloud-a). p99 tail spikes during initial KV population were reduced by ~40%.
- L40S PCIe5 (cloud-d) delivered the highest sustainable tokens/sec at steady-state in FP16 for batched scenarios (B>4), but had larger variance during KV append bursts: p95 increased by ~18% relative to H100 NVLink.
- H100 PCIe variant (cloud-c) showed both higher jitter and unexpected kernel-launch serialization with the tested driver (CUDA 12.1 / driver 535.x) — likely an interplay between driver and 2nd-gen NVLink absence.
- Driver/CUDA differences: CUDA 12.2 + driver 545.x improved host->device memcpy throughput by measurable amounts on PCIe5 L40S nodes, reducing some cold-start latency, but did not eliminate NVLink advantage for low-batch streaming tail reduction.
- Across all SKUs the dominant root cause for initial p99 spikes was the host memcpy + kernel scheduling window for the first KV block appends (not model compute), especially when application-level prefetch was disabled.
detailed_findings:
1) Host memcpy vs kernel dispatch: CUPTI capture shows that on PCIe SKUs, memcpy host->device occupied 25-40ms in some cold-start traces when context extension involved >64KB of KV payloads; on NVLink H100 the same memcpy windows were 8-12ms. The kernel dispatch lag (time from memcpy end to first kernel launch touching new KV) correlated strongly with observed p99 latency spikes.

2) PCIe Gen5 behavior (L40S): sustained bandwidth peaks were higher and throughput matched NVLink for bulk transfers, but memcpy latency variance was higher under multi-threaded driver paths (we saw interleaving with other CUDA consumers causing serialization). This explains why steady-state throughput is great but transient warmup is noisy.

3) Driver & CUDA interplay: older driver (535.x) on H100 PCIe showed serialized cuLaunch latency under certain small-kernel patterns that our runtime emits during KV updates. Upgrading to 545.x reduced launch overhead by ~20-30% in microbenchmarks.

4) KV eviction cost: when eviction kicks in (context > soft cap), the platform issues more device memory churn and host-device shuffling. On A100 PCIe nodes eviction caused a noticeable p99 amplification (up to 2x baseline p99), whereas NVLink nodes amortized eviction cost better due to lower memcopy latencies.

5) Small-batch streaming (B=1): NVLink H100 reduced frequency of tail spikes meaningfully, which in practice reduces client-side retry/backoff events. For B>=4 the interconnect matters less; kernel compute dominates.

6) Observed micro-pattern: many p99 events align with a short-lived spike in PCIe traffic followed by a GPU idle window (kernel queue starvation) — suggests host CPU scheduling and driver submission path are key levers.

Representative numbers (median of multiple runs):
- cloud-b (H100 NVLink) cold->steady median first_token latency: 42ms (FP16, B=1)
- cloud-a (A100 PCIe) same config: 48ms
- cloud-d (L40S PCIe5) same config: 45ms but p99 variance higher (+20ms p99 tail).
Driver impact: driver 545.x reduced cold memcpy medians by ~6-8ms on PCIe5 nodes vs 535.x.

Notes on reproducibility: raw CUPTI traces and host logs are in linked artifacts GH PR; we captured ~2GB of trace per SKU for the sample window.
implications_for_runtime:
- For low-latency streaming workloads we should enable conservative background prefetching of next-KV-blocks on PCIe SKUs to hide memcpy latency; this will reduce p99 at the cost of some extra memory pressure.
- Implement driver/version detection and apply runtime heuristics: enable small-batch kernel coalescing and submission batching on SKUs with known cuLaunch serialization issues.
- Prefer client-side concurrency shaping for PCIe-only nodes: small bursts should be smoothed at the gateway to avoid host-side memcpy storms.
- Add automatic per-SKU telemetry-driven warmup policies in the serving runtime: e.g., on first N requests do speculative KV prefetch if measured host-copy latency exceeds a threshold.
- For Dedicated offering, include recommended SKU+driver matrix for streaming use-cases (H100 NVLink preferred for stringent tail requirements; L40S for bulk throughput workloads).
next_steps:
- Run controlled experiments with application-level prefetch enabled (vary prefetch window sizes) on all SKUs and measure net gain/loss in p50/p95/p99.
- Expand model matrix to 70B-ish sparse-attention variants to see if kernel-launch dynamics scale similarly.
- Re-run H100 PCIe variant tests after driver upgrade and with different CPU configs to rule out host scheduler interference.
- Prototype runtime submission coalescing and measure impact on p99 (short A/B).
- Collate artifacts and prepare a short internal playbook recommending SKU/driver combos for customers with streaming long-context SLAs.
unresolved_questions:
- Is the observed kernel serialization on H100 PCIe purely a driver/device feature, or does our small-kernel emission pattern exacerbate it? Need deeper CUPTI kernel-level stacks.
- How will multi-tenant noisy neighbors on shared clouds change the memcpy variance observed here? We tested mostly isolated instances.
- What are the exact NVLink telemetry counters we can expose in-prod to trigger runtime warmup heuristics automatically?
- Tradeoffs: how much memory budget should prefetching consume before it negatively impacts steady-state throughput across quantized models?
